strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and underexplored semi-supervised vision-language alignment setting bridging fully supervised CLIP-style training and fully unsupervised alignment, with clear practical relevance for low-resource domains.

Provides a genuine theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1/C.4): an explicit closed-form gradient for the proposed KLOT divergence, derived via entropic OT duality and the envelope theorem, removing the memory bottleneck of Sinkhorn unrolling and outperforming implicit differentiation in speed/memory (demonstrated empirically in Fig. 3/6).

Extensive and systematic empirical evaluation: ablations over linear alignment methods (Procrustes, CCA, contrastive) and divergences (CKA, InfoNCE, KLOT), robustness studies over number of paired/unpaired samples, unpaired data source, supervised data source, and choice of unimodal encoders (DINOv2/v3, multiple LLM text encoders).

Careful baseline construction: adapts several existing supervised/semi-supervised methods (SAIL, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE) to the proposed setting with hyperparameter tuning, and SOTAlign consistently and often substantially outperforms them across COCO/Flickr30k retrieval and multiple zero-shot classification benchmarks.

Introduces a principled and scalable proxy (total spherical sliced Wasserstein distance) for predicting when unpaired data will help, and shows a strong empirical correlation with downstream gains, adding interpretability to the method's behavior under distribution shift.

Provides closed-form derivations for the linear alignment models (Procrustes, CCA) and detailed proofs in the appendix, along with thorough implementation details (hyperparameters, encoders, datasets) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains far below the fully supervised upper bound (e.g., 46.1% vs 56.4% ImageNet top-1, Table 5), and the practical usefulness of the semi-supervised regime versus simply collecting more paired data is not deeply analyzed (e.g., cost-benefit tradeoffs).

The main results rely predominantly on a single default encoder pair (DINOv3 ViT-L + NV-Embed-v2) and a single primary unpaired source (CC3M); while robustness studies exist, they are comparatively limited in scale (fewer seeds/error bars) and the core benchmarking tables (Tables 4-6) lack variance estimates or statistical significance testing.

Adapted baselines (STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP) were not originally designed for this exact setting, and while the authors tune their hyperparameters, it is unclear whether the adaptations are optimally implemented, raising some concern about baseline fairness/strength.

The theoretical contribution, while useful in practice, is an incremental extension of known entropic OT duality results (closely related to prior work such as Van Assel et al. 2023 and the cited blog post by Assel 2024), somewhat limiting its novelty as a standalone theoretical result.

The comparison with SUE (Table 6/11) is conducted on a very different, much smaller evaluation protocol (400 test samples, per-dataset training) which limits the strength of claims about generalizing beyond SUE's setting.

Epsilon/entropic-regularization hyperparameters for KLOT (0.01 reference space, 0.05 joint space) and other design choices (SigLIP init, pooling scheme) appear to be fixed via limited manual tuning without a systematic sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns for new domains/encoders.

The claim that linear alignment models provide strong support for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis is somewhat anecdotal; deeper analysis (e.g., relating alignment quality to representation geometry beyond mutual k-NN correlation) would strengthen this framing.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored setting (semi-supervised alignment of frozen unimodal encoders with abundant unpaired data), and clearly motivates it against fully-supervised contrastive VLM training.

The engineering contribution around avoiding Sinkhorn unrolling/implicit differentiation via an explicit closed-form gradient for the KLOT divergence is useful and is empirically shown to yield large memory and runtime savings (Fig. 3, Fig. 6), which could benefit other OT-based training pipelines.

Extensive empirical study: ablations over linear teacher choice (Procrustes/CCA/contrastive) crossed with divergence choice (CKA/InfoNCE/KLOT), robustness to number of paired/unpaired samples, encoder combinations, cross-dataset unpaired sources, and a sensible distance-based analysis (spherical sliced Wasserstein) correlating distribution shift with performance gains.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details (hyperparameters, optimizer, encoders, batch composition) are given in the appendix, and closed-form derivations for Procrustes/CCA variants are provided with proofs.

Comparisons span multiple downstream tasks (retrieval on COCO/Flickr30k, zero-shot classification on 7 datasets) and multiple existing methods adapted as baselines (SAIL, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE), which is more comprehensive than prior semi-supervised alignment papers that are restricted to single datasets/tasks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result (Theorem 5.1/C.4) is essentially a direct application of the standard envelope theorem to entropic OT duality (a well-known fact in the OT literature, e.g., Peyré & Cuturi 2019, and acknowledged similar derivations exist, e.g., Assel 2024 blog post cited by the authors themselves). Presenting this as a headline theoretical contribution somewhat overstates its novelty relative to its true incremental nature, even though the practical memory/speed benefit is real.

Most main comparison tables (Tables 1–6, 7–11) report single-run numbers with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing, despite some gaps between methods being small (e.g., STRUCTURE vs SAIL in Table 4/5, or divergence comparisons in Table 1). This makes it difficult to assess whether reported gains are robust or within run-to-run variance, especially given the small-sample (10k pairs) regime, which is likely to be noisy.

Because no established baselines exist for this exact semi-supervised setting, all baselines (SAIL semi-sup variant, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE) were reimplemented and tuned by the authors themselves. This creates a real risk of asymmetric optimization effort favoring the proposed method; the surprisingly large gaps versus SUE in Table 6/11 (e.g., 55.3 vs 22.8 R@5 on Polyvore) in particular warrant more scrutiny/validation against the original SUE implementation or reported numbers.

The justification for the two-stage design (linear teacher regularizing a nonlinear model via KLOT) is largely empirical/intuitive rather than theoretically grounded; there is no formal argument for why regularizing toward a linear teacher's geometry with an OT-based KL avoids underfitting/overfitting relative to alternative regularization schemes, beyond the ablation table.

The hyperparameter α is selected via grid search using retrieval performance on a validation split, which is reasonable but somewhat softens the semi-supervised/low-resource framing, since tuning still implicitly leverages more labeled signal (validation retrieval) than the nominal 'few pairs' would suggest in a truly resource-constrained deployment.

The Impact/limitations discussion is extremely thin (a single sentence stating no specific societal impacts), which is weak for a paper whose central claims relate to representation alignment and could have implications for bias propagation from pretrained unimodal encoders into the aligned multimodal space; failure modes (e.g., complete failure at 100 pairs) are noted but not analyzed in depth.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis motivation, while intuitive, is not tested rigorously beyond correlational evidence (e.g., mutual k-NN vs performance, Fig. 9, with only 6 data points), so claims that the method 'provides empirical support' for the hypothesis are somewhat overreaching given the limited number of encoder pairs evaluated.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: aligning frozen unimodal vision/language encoders under severe paired-data scarcity while exploiting abundant unpaired data, directly testing the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

The proposed KLOT divergence is a principled generalization of the OT-CLIP/InfoNCE perspective to non-identity target transport plans, and is well motivated relative to CKA (too rigid) and generalized InfoNCE (too coarse, only preserves argmax).

Theorem 5.1 provides a genuinely useful closed-form gradient for the OT-based divergence, removing the memory bottleneck of Sinkhorn unrolling and the runtime cost of implicit differentiation; this is empirically validated with clear, convincing memory/runtime plots (Figure 3, Figure 6) and is likely to be broadly useful for other OT-based contrastive/alignment methods.

Extensive and carefully designed experiments: ablations over linear teacher choice x divergence choice (Table 1), robustness to number of paired/unpaired samples (Figure 4, 7, 8), robustness to encoder pairs (Table 3, 8) with a plausible connection between mutual k-NN similarity and downstream performance, and a novel and useful quantification of distribution shift via spherical sliced Wasserstein distance that correlates strongly with performance gains (Figure 5, 10, 11).

Strong and fair baseline implementation: the authors adapt SAIL, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, and SUE to the semi-supervised setting with hyperparameter tuning, and SOTAlign consistently and substantially outperforms all of them across retrieval and classification tasks and multiple datasets (Tables 4-6, 9-11).

Good reproducibility: implementation details (optimizer, batch sizes, epsilon values, encoder choices, architecture) and dataset details are thoroughly documented in the appendix, and compute requirements are modest (single A100 GPU).
weaknesses: Statistical rigor for the main benchmark tables (Table 4, 5, 6) is unclear -- no error bars/variance across seeds are reported for these headline comparisons, even though some robustness figures do show shaded regions; it is hard to assess the significance of gains such as the marginal differences between STRUCTURE variants.

The main results rely predominantly on a single encoder pair (DINOv3 + NV-Embed-v2); while Table 3/8 explore other encoders, most of the qualitative analysis (data source, distribution shift, benchmarking) is done only with this one pair, leaving open how much conclusions generalize to other/weaker encoder combinations.

The choice of regularization weight α is selected using retrieval performance on CC3M, which is close to the training/target distribution; this raises a mild concern about how much hyperparameter tuning benefits from implicit access to target-like validation signal compared to baselines, though the paper does show robustness to different α in Section 6.2.

The core theoretical contribution (envelope-theorem-based gradient for entropic OT) is closely related to prior results (Van Assel et al. 2023, Uscidda & Cuturi 2023, and an informal blog post by one author), and this connection, while acknowledged, is somewhat downplayed in the main text relative to how central it is to the paper's claimed novelty.

Table 1 shows that using the natural 'Contrastive' linear teacher with KLOT actually underperforms CCA+KLOT (28.5 vs 30.3), which is slightly counterintuitive given contrastive learning is the dominant paradigm; the paper does not deeply investigate why the simplest closed-form linear methods outperform the contrastively learned teacher.

The Impact Statement is minimal and does not meaningfully engage with the potential implications (positive or negative) of enabling VLM construction with drastically less paired supervision, e.g., in specialized or sensitive domains mentioned in the intro.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously solves a genuine computational bottleneck in OT-based alignment losses: Theorem 5.1 provides a closed-form expression for the gradient of the KLOT divergence via the envelope theorem, removing the need for Sinkhorn unrolling or costly implicit differentiation, with clear empirical demonstration (Fig. 3, Fig. 8) of large memory and runtime savings.

Very extensive and carefully designed experimental evaluation: ablations on number of paired/unpaired samples, choice of linear teacher and divergence, entropic regularization parameters, robustness to noisy teacher pairs, cross-dataset distribution shift quantified via a novel total spherical sliced Wasserstein distance metric that correlates strongly with downstream performance (Pearson r up to -0.99).

Strong and fair baseline suite adapted specifically to the proposed semi-supervised setting (SAIL, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE), with SOTAlign consistently outperforming them across retrieval and classification benchmarks and multiple encoder combinations.
Demonstrates generalization beyond vision-language to other domains/modalities (satellite imagery via SkyScript, speech-text via LibriSpeech/WavLM), strengthening claims of broad applicability.
Practically useful auxiliary finding that mutual k-NN similarity between frozen unimodal encoders strongly predicts downstream alignment quality (Pearson r = 0.95), offering a cheap diagnostic tool.

Reasonably reproducible: architectural and optimization details, hyperparameter search ranges, and dataset descriptions are given in appendices; closed-form solutions for linear alignment models (Procrustes, CCA) are derived explicitly.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is somewhat incremental, combining existing ingredients (Platonic Representation Hypothesis-motivated frozen-encoder alignment, generalized InfoNCE/OT-CLIP's inverse OT view, and Snekhorn-style OT divergences) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the main technical novelty is the gradient derivation, which is a relatively narrow (though useful) result.

A persistent and fairly large performance gap remains versus fully supervised training with 1M pairs (e.g., 46.1 vs 56.4 top-1 ImageNet accuracy, 26.5 vs 35.5 COCO T2I R@1), which somewhat tempers the practical significance of the semi-supervised approach for high-accuracy applications.

Hyperparameters (α, ε, ε*, choice of linear teacher/divergence) are selected via grid search on retrieval performance on CC3M/COCO validation splits that overlap with the evaluation distributions used later, raising some concern about optimistic tuning and reducing confidence in out-of-the-box applicability without dataset-specific retuning.

Most main results tables (1–7) report single-run numbers without confidence intervals or multiple seeds, making it harder to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, although some appendix figures do include shaded uncertainty bands.

The method still requires a small set of paired examples and its behavior appears to fail below ~100–1000 pairs (as shown in Figure 5/9), so the claimed applicability to extremely low-resource domains is bounded and not fully characterized.

The Impact Statement is minimal/boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential downstream risks of easier construction of VLMs from limited paired data (e.g., in sensitive domains), despite the paper explicitly targeting specialized/medical/industrial use cases.

strengths: Introduces and clearly formalizes a practically relevant semi-supervised alignment setting (few paired samples + abundant unpaired unimodal data) that is underexplored relative to fully supervised or fully unsupervised alignment.

Solid theoretical contribution: an explicit closed-form gradient for the proposed KLOT divergence (Theorem 5.1/C.4), derived via the envelope theorem, which removes the memory bottleneck of Sinkhorn unrolling and is empirically shown to be substantially more memory- and time-efficient than unrolling or implicit differentiation (Figure 3, Figure 8).

Extensive empirical validation across many axes: number of paired/unpaired samples, unpaired data source and domain shift, choice of unimodal encoder pairs, multiple divergences, and multiple linear teacher variants (Procrustes, CCA, contrastive), lending some robustness to the core claims.

Interesting auxiliary findings that connect to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, e.g., the strong correlation (Pearson r=0.95) between pre-training mutual k-NN similarity of frozen encoders and downstream alignment performance, and the correlation between spherical sliced Wasserstein distance and performance gains from unpaired data (r up to -0.99).
Generalization experiments beyond the core vision-language retrieval/classification setting (satellite imagery, speech-text) suggest the method is not narrowly tailored to one domain.
Reasonably broad baseline suite (SAIL, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE) with consistent gains reported across retrieval and classification tasks.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is incremental: it largely recombines existing ideas (OT-CLIP's inverse-OT view of InfoNCE, Sinkhorn/entropic-OT divergences from Van Assel et al. 2023, S-CLIP's OT-based pseudo-labeling, linear alignment via CCA/Procrustes) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the explicit-gradient result, while useful, is a fairly direct consequence of well-known entropic-OT duality/envelope-theorem arguments.

Because the semi-supervised setting is new, most 'baselines' (semi-supervised SAIL, semi-supervised STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP adaptations) are reimplemented/adapted by the authors themselves for this setting, with hyperparameters tuned by the same team; this raises a risk of implementation or tuning bias favoring the proposed method, and no independent verification is possible.

Absolute performance remains far below the fully supervised upper bound even in the best settings (e.g., Table 4: SOTAlign COCO T2I 26.5 vs. SAIL trained on 1M pairs at 35.5), which somewhat tempers the practical significance of the claimed gains despite large relative improvements over weak low-resource baselines.

Main result tables (Tables 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10) report single-run numbers without seeds, confidence intervals, or variance, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially since some gaps between methods are modest (e.g., 1-2 points in several classification/retrieval comparisons).

The method carries considerable hyperparameter complexity (entropic regularization epsilon/epsilon*, ratio tuning, alpha selection via validation retrieval, choice of linear teacher and divergence) with only heuristic guidelines provided, which may hinder reproducibility and practical adoption without extensive tuning.

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence fully supports, e.g., 'the first model that can effectively leverage large-scale unimodal data for multimodal alignment in this setting' understates the closeness of S-CLIP and SUE's contributions, and 'fully address the memory bottlenecks' for OT-based methods is a strong claim given the result is specific to the KL-based KLOT formulation.

Dependence on the compatibility of the two pretrained encoders (per the mutual k-NN analysis) is a real limitation; the paper does not deeply explore failure cases or provide guidance for practitioners when encoders are poorly aligned, beyond correlational diagnostics.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: semi-supervised alignment of frozen unimodal vision/language encoders with scarce paired data but abundant unpaired data, directly testing the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

Solid theoretical contribution: derives a closed-form gradient for the proposed KLOT optimal-transport divergence (Theorem 5.1/C.4), removing the memory bottleneck of Sinkhorn unrolling and avoiding the runtime cost of implicit differentiation, with clean proofs provided in the appendix and empirical validation of memory/speed gains (Fig. 3, Fig. 8).

Extensive and systematic experimentation: ablations over linear teacher choice, divergence choice, entropic regularization schedule, number of paired/unpaired samples, data source/domain shift, and choice of unimodal encoders, with many results replicated in the appendix.

Interesting and practically useful auxiliary findings, e.g., that simple closed-form linear alignment (CCA/Procrustes) already recovers meaningful cross-modal structure from very few pairs, and that mutual k-NN between frozen encoders strongly correlates (r=0.95) with downstream alignment quality, offering a cheap diagnostic tool.

Good breadth of comparisons against adapted supervised/semi-supervised baselines (SAIL, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE) across multiple tasks (retrieval, classification) and datasets, plus generalization experiments to remote sensing (SkyScript) and speech-text (LibriSpeech), showing the framework is not narrowly tied to vision-language alone.
Quantitative analysis linking distribution shift (via a total spherical sliced-Wasserstein distance) to downstream performance gains, providing a principled explanation for when unpaired data helps.
weaknesses: Several semi-supervised baselines (SAIL semi-sup variant, STRUCTURE with unpaired data) are extensions implemented by the authors themselves rather than established prior methods for this exact setting, which could bias the comparison in SOTAlign's favor; independent verification of baseline tuning thoroughness is hard to assess from the text alone.

Selection of the regularization weight α is based on retrieval performance on a validation-like split of CC3M, and hyperparameter search ranges are reported mainly for SOTAlign; it is not entirely clear that baselines received comparably exhaustive tuning, which slightly weakens the fairness of the head-to-head comparison.

Absolute downstream numbers remain modest compared to fully supervised CLIP-scale models (e.g., 46.1% ImageNet top-1 vs. supervised SAIL at 1M pairs reaching 56.4%, and vs. CLIP-level performance in the 70%+ range), so while the relative gains over the semi-supervised regime are convincing, the practical significance for production-level zero-shot systems is still limited.

Main result tables (e.g., Table 4, 5) do not report variance/confidence intervals across random seeds, making it harder to judge the statistical significance of the reported gains, despite some seed-averaged results being shown for the distribution-shift analysis.

The core theoretical device (KLOT gradient via envelope theorem for entropic OT) builds closely on prior work (OT-CLIP, Snekhorn, Monge Gap), so while the explicit derivation and its systematic application here are valuable, the underlying mathematical idea is more of a targeted extension than an entirely new theoretical framework.

Method description partially conflates the pretrained encoder choice with the alignment method's performance; because absolute results are quite sensitive to the specific backbone pair (as shown in Table 3/10), it's unclear how robust the reported gains are for weaker or more heterogeneous encoder pairs in real deployment scenarios beyond the curated experiments shown.
